meta.theme: prohibitions explained by what will not fit a community's scheme of kinds rather than by danger, supported by rules on people in transition and by how prohibitions end, and limited by the author's own warning that the account works only where the scheme is established before the list

meta.reviewer_notes: A thesis with three supports of different kinds and a final paragraph that turns on the thesis itself. The discarded hygiene account is stated generously in the first paragraph and is then available as a wrong answer in four of the six questions, which is the point of stating it so well. 2026-10-03 CAT-size pass: 729→499 words, 6→5 paragraphs, 6→4 questions. Merged the third support (how prohibitions end) into the evidence paragraph instead of losing it, and tightened throughout. Kept application, inference, title and strengthen; dropped the EXCEPT question and the role-of-detail question, whose explanation names a paragraph that no longer exists.

quality.adversarial_review: The hygiene account is the live rival in four questions because the first paragraph gives it its best form and never calls it foolish. Q1's exception is the statement about rules learned in childhood, which is plausible everywhere and appears nowhere in the second paragraph's three objections. Q2's rival is the option saying the human cases are conceded as resistant, which reverses their role: the passage calls them the clearest evidence and the nearest thing to a controlled comparison. Q3's rival is the hygiene explanation applied to the dog, refused by the second paragraph's finding that prohibition and danger do not line up. Q4's rival is the option that a prohibition ends when nobody can say why it exists, whereas the fifth paragraph makes the end depend on the classification ceasing to organise anything and says prohibitions are very seldom repealed on evidence. Q5's rival is the title about rules outliving their reasons, which is the hygiene account's own account of survival. Q6's rival is the finding that prohibited animals carry no disease, which is already in the second paragraph as an objection to hygiene and does nothing for the scheme; the key supplies the prediction in advance that the sixth paragraph says the account needs. (2026-10-03, CAT-size pass: q1, q2 were dropped, so any note above about them no longer applies.)

paragraphs.text: Most people first reach for a practical explanation. Prohibitions on certain foods and kinds of contact are taken to be old public health. Someone noticed that a meat sickened people in hot weather, the observation hardened into a prohibition, and the prohibition outlived its reason. The account is attractive because it is generous: it credits the ancestors with being right about the world.

It does not survive even a glance at the lists. Many prohibited things carry no particular danger, and many dangerous things are not prohibited. Where rules are graded, they are often kept most strictly by those least exposed to the supposed danger: priests, the old, those who have left the fields. And practices that genuinely reduce danger, such as treating water or handling meat in heat, are almost never prohibited. They are passed on as skill, judged by results, and replaced when a better method appears, which is not how a taboo behaves.

The pattern becomes visible as soon as one asks not what is dangerous but what is anomalous. Every community sorts the world before it does anything else: creatures of the water, of the air, of the ground; kin and stranger; the living and the dead. The scheme is rarely written down, and is all the more binding for that. What attracts unease, and then rules, is whatever refuses to sit inside a single division of it: a creature that lives in water and breathes air, or one that comes into the house and was never domesticated. A prohibition of this kind is not protecting a body. It is protecting a scheme.

The clearest evidence lies where no question of contagion can arise at all. Communities that prohibit nothing in their diet will still surround a mourner with restrictions, or a bride between two households, or a traveller newly returned. Nothing here is alleged to be catching, yet the rules have the shape of the food rules: separation, avoidance, and a closing rite that returns the person to one category. How such rules end tells the same story. They lapse when the classification that produced them stops organising anything: a prohibition attached to a distinction between two kinds of kin fades once households cease to arrange themselves by it, without anybody deciding that the forbidden thing was safe. Prohibitions are very seldom repealed on evidence.

The account has a weakness of its own, and it is not the one usually brought against it. It can be applied to anything after the event. Tell me a creature is forbidden and I will find a boundary it sits across, since every creature sits across one if the scheme is described loosely enough. So the explanation is worth something only where the scheme was established first, from other evidence such as language, household or calendar. Where that has been done, the prohibitions have often been predicted rather than merely accounted for. Where it has not, the categorical account redescribes a list and calls the redescription a reason.

questions.target_mistake: applying the explanation the passage rejects because the new case involves an animal and a wash, which makes contagion the obvious frame
questions.prediction_target: The learner should extract the rule first: prohibition falls on what straddles a division of the community's own scheme, not on what is dirty.
questions.stem: A community keeps dogs outside the house, feeds them apart from the family and requires a wash after touching one, while handling visibly dirtier livestock under no such rule. On the author's account, the most promising explanation is that

options.A: the dog sits between the household and the wild in a scheme that provides no place for it
options.B: the community once learned that dogs carried an illness and has kept the rule ever since
options.C: the community's scheme of categories is stricter than those of the communities near it
options.D: the community must at some point have had a rule of the same kind about another animal

explanation.expert_notice: The case is built so that danger is ruled out by the facts given: the livestock is dirtier and carries no rule. That is the second paragraph's objection in miniature, and it leaves only the third paragraph's test, which asks what will not sit inside a single division of the scheme.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option runs that test on the case. The third paragraph names an animal that comes into the house and was never domesticated as a standard anomaly, and the dog described here is exactly that: attached to the household, admitted to its edges, and never absorbed into it. The prohibition marks a creature the scheme cannot place, which is why the dirtier animal, securely placed, attracts nothing.
explanation.question_type_note: Application questions want the author's rule run mechanically on a case he never saw. Extract the rule in one sentence before reading the options, or the case's surface will suggest the explanation the passage rejected.
explanation.reading_habit: When a new case is described, notice which facts have been put there to switch an explanation off. A detail like the dirtier animal under no rule is a signal, not scenery.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the hygiene account from the first paragraph, and the case as described defeats it in the same way the second paragraph does: the animal that carries the visible danger carries no rule.
distractors.seductive_element: Washing after contact is so plainly a health measure that the reader supplies a health explanation before noticing that the livestock detail has ruled it out.

distractors.why_wrong: No comparison between neighbouring communities appears in the passage or in the case. The author's account explains which items a scheme prohibits, not why one community should prohibit more than another.
distractors.seductive_element: Strictness is the most visible feature of the case, and a comparison seems the natural way to explain a strong rule.

distractors.why_wrong: Nothing in the account requires a history of similar rules. The explanation works from the shape of the present scheme, and the fourth paragraph's only claim about history concerns how prohibitions end rather than what must have preceded them.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage does discuss prohibitions across time, which makes a historical claim sound like the kind of thing it would say.

questions.target_mistake: supposing that a rule ends when its reason is lost, when the passage makes the end depend on the classification ceasing to matter
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that what ends a prohibition is a change in the scheme rather than a discovery about the thing prohibited.
questions.stem: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?

options.A: A prohibition comes to an end at the moment when the thing prohibited is shown to be harmless.
options.B: A prohibition ends once a community has found a safer way of handling the thing.
options.C: A prohibition ends when those who keep it can no longer say why it exists.
options.D: A change in how households are arranged can end a rule that proof of safety would not.

explanation.expert_notice: The fourth paragraph ends with two statements and they have to be held together. Prohibitions lapse when the classification that produced them stops organising anything, and prohibitions are very seldom repealed on evidence. One route works and the other does not.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option puts those two together in a single case. The paragraph's own example is a prohibition attached to a distinction between two kinds of kin, which fades once households cease to arrange themselves by it and fades without anybody having decided the thing was safe. A rearrangement of households therefore does what a demonstration of safety does not.
explanation.question_type_note: Where a passage names one thing that ends a practice and one thing that does not, the inference question will usually ask you to keep both. Options that offer only the discarded route are the standard decoys.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author says something is seldom done on evidence, write down what it is done on instead. The replacement is the half of the sentence that questions are built from.

distractors.why_wrong: The fourth paragraph rules this out in a sentence of its own: prohibitions are very seldom repealed on evidence, and the example fades without anybody having decided that the forbidden thing was safe.
distractors.seductive_element: It is how rules end in the reader's own experience, and the hygiene account of the first paragraph invites exactly this picture of discovery and revision.

distractors.why_wrong: Safer handling belongs to the second paragraph, where techniques for water and meat are said to be replaced when a better method appears. That is contrasted with taboo rather than offered as a way of ending one.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage does discuss improvement of method, and improvement sounds like the kind of thing that makes a prohibition unnecessary.

distractors.why_wrong: Losing the reason is part of the first paragraph's story of survival, where a prohibition outlives its reason and persists. The passage makes survival compatible with forgetting and makes the end depend on the classification instead.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because forgetting the reason really is in the passage, and a rule nobody can justify does feel like a rule about to disappear.

questions.target_mistake: titling the passage from the account it rejects, or from the single kind of prohibition that occupies its first two paragraphs
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: a title must name what the prohibitions have in common, which is that they fall on whatever the scheme cannot place.
questions.stem: Which of the following would be the most appropriate title for the passage?

options.A: The Hidden Wisdom of Ancient Food Rules
options.B: Why Some Animals Are Never Eaten
options.C: Rules for Things That Will Not Fit
options.D: The Rules That Outlived Their Reasons

explanation.expert_notice: The third paragraph gives the thesis in one line, that what attracts unease and then rules is whatever refuses to sit inside a single division of the scheme, and the fourth paragraph extends it to people and to the way prohibitions end. A title has to cover all of that.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct title names the common property the passage argues for and nothing else. It reaches the food rules, the mourner, the bride and the returning traveller, since all of them are cases of something that cannot be placed in one category, and it leaves room for the closing warning, which is about how such a claim must be tested rather than about what it says.
explanation.question_type_note: A title is the main idea under a word limit, so the altitude matters more than the wording. Too low and it names one class of case; too high or too sympathetic and it names the account the passage discarded.
explanation.reading_habit: Ask what each candidate title would exclude. A title that has no room for half the passage's evidence has named a paragraph rather than an argument.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the hygiene account, which the second paragraph dismantles with three objections. The passage credits it with being generous rather than with being right.
distractors.seductive_element: The first paragraph states the account warmly and at length, and a title drawn from an opening paragraph is a familiar mistake.

distractors.why_wrong: Food is the way in, not the subject. The last two paragraphs are about mourners, brides, travellers, kinship distinctions and the conditions under which a claim of this kind can be tested.
distractors.seductive_element: Food prohibitions are what the reader came in expecting and what the first two paragraphs discuss.

distractors.why_wrong: Outliving the reason is the hygiene account's own explanation of how a rule survives, stated in the first paragraph. As a title it would name the position the passage exists to replace.
distractors.seductive_element: It is a memorable phrase from the passage and describes something the passage does say happens, which makes it feel authorised.

questions.target_mistake: strengthening the case against hygiene, which the passage has already made, instead of the case for the scheme, which is what the last paragraph says still needs support
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that the strengthener will be a scheme established independently and then used to predict a list, which is the test the final paragraph demands.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's account?

options.A: A scheme of kinds worked out from one community's language alone predicted its forbidden animals.
options.B: Many of the animals prohibited in such communities are found by modern study to carry no disease.
options.C: Prohibitions are most often lifted once a forbidden animal has been shown to be safe to eat.
options.D: The rules are taught to children long before they are old enough to ask what they are for.

explanation.expert_notice: The last paragraph states the condition a strengthener must satisfy. Because the account can be applied to anything after the event, it is worth something only where the scheme is established first and from other evidence, so that prohibitions are predicted rather than merely accounted for.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that condition met. The scheme comes from the language alone, which is independent of the list, and the list then follows from it in advance. That closes the loophole the author himself opened, since a description arrived at without knowing the answer cannot have been bent to fit the answer.
explanation.question_type_note: When an author names the weakness of his own case, a strengthen question is almost always asking for the thing that repairs that weakness. Read the final paragraph before the options.
explanation.reading_habit: Ask which claim in the passage is still unsupported after the last paragraph. The strengthener attaches to that claim, not to the one the author has already established at length.

distractors.why_wrong: This is already the second paragraph's first objection, and it only damages the rival. Showing that prohibited animals are harmless leaves entirely open whether the scheme of kinds explains which ones were chosen.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because damaging a rival feels like supporting the survivor, and this is the passage's own most quotable piece of evidence.

distractors.why_wrong: The fourth paragraph says the opposite, that prohibitions are very seldom repealed on evidence and instead lapse when the classification stops organising anything. This would undo one of the author's three supports.
distractors.seductive_element: It reads like a fact about how customs modernise, and modernising by evidence is the shape most readers expect such a fact to have.

distractors.why_wrong: Early teaching is compatible with every account of where the rules came from, including the one the passage rejects, so it cannot favour either. The dispute is about which items are chosen, not about when they are learned.
distractors.seductive_element: It sounds like support for the claim that the scheme is absorbed rather than reasoned out, which the third paragraph does say of the scheme itself.

vocabulary.passage_use: not what is dangerous but what is anomalous
vocabulary.meaning_here: not fitting the categories a community already works with

vocabulary.passage_use: where no question of contagion can arise at all
vocabulary.meaning_here: the passing of illness from one body to another

vocabulary.passage_use: They lapse when the classification that produced them stops organising anything
vocabulary.meaning_here: fall out of use quietly, without being formally abolished

mentor.challenge: A familiar explanation is set out generously and then taken apart, and a replacement is supported three separate ways. The last paragraph criticises the replacement; do not mistake that for abandoning it.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: Prohibitions are better explained by what will not fit a community's scheme of kinds than by danger, since prohibition and harm do not line up, since the same rules appear where no illness could be alleged, and since such rules end when the classification stops mattering rather than when the thing is shown to be safe, though the account only earns its keep where the scheme is described before the list.
mentor.main_idea: The hygiene story about taboos fails because prohibited things are often harmless, dangerous things often unprohibited, and genuinely protective practices are treated as technique rather than as taboo. Prohibitions instead fall on whatever straddles a boundary in a community's scheme of categories. Rules for people in transition and the way prohibitions fade both support this. The author then warns that the account is too easy to apply after the fact and works only where the scheme is established independently.
mentor.simple_explanation:
Why do communities forbid certain foods, or certain kinds of contact?

The usual answer is health. Long ago someone noticed that a food made people ill, the warning became a rule, and the rule survived after everyone forgot the reason. It is a kind explanation, because it makes the ancestors sound sensible.

But look at the actual lists. Lots of forbidden things are perfectly safe, and lots of dangerous things are not forbidden. Where the rules come in degrees, the strictest keepers are often the people furthest from the danger, such as priests and the old. And the practices that genuinely do protect you, like treating water properly, are not taboos at all. They are skills. People judge them by whether they work and replace them when something better turns up, which is exactly what nobody does with a taboo.

So ask a different question. Not what is dangerous, but what does not fit. Every community sorts the world first: water creatures, air creatures, ground creatures; family and stranger; living and dead. The sorting is usually unwritten, which makes it stronger rather than weaker. And the things that make people uneasy, and end up with rules round them, are the ones that will not sit in a single box. Something that lives in water and breathes air. An animal that comes into the house but was never tamed. The rule is guarding the sorting, not the body.

The strongest evidence is where illness is not even on the table. Communities with no food rules at all still hedge a mourner about with restrictions, or a bride between two houses, or someone just back from a journey. Nobody claims any of this is catching. Yet the rules look identical: stay apart, do not touch certain things, and end with a ceremony that puts the person firmly back in one category. The way these rules end points the same way. They do not end when someone proves the thing is safe. They fade when the division they protected stops mattering, for instance when households stop organising themselves around a distinction between kinds of relative.

Then the author turns on his own theory. Its problem is that it is too easy. Tell me anything is forbidden and I can find some boundary it crosses, if I am allowed to describe the boundaries loosely. So the theory is only worth having when someone works out the scheme first, from the language or the household or the calendar, and then predicts what will be forbidden. Done that way it has often been right. Done the other way it is just a fancier way of reading out the list.
mentor.why_difficult: The rejected explanation is stated so well that it stays available as an answer for the rest of the passage, and it is the explanation every reader already holds. The second difficulty is the last paragraph, which criticises the author's own account: a reader who has been following the argument may read that criticism as a retraction, and a reader who has not may miss that it sets a condition the strengthen question depends on. The three supports are also of three different kinds, and readers who register only the first will find the questions about the other two unanswerable.
mentor.author_intention: To replace an explanation that feels charitable with one that actually fits the lists, and then to make the reader distrust the new explanation in the one way it deserves to be distrusted.

paragraph_journey.note: Taboos as forgotten public health: someone noticed a danger, the rule survived, the reason did not. Attractive because it makes the ancestors right.
Harmless things are forbidden and dangerous ones are not; the strictest keepers are the least exposed; and genuinely protective practices are treated as skill, not as taboo.
Ask what is anomalous rather than what is dangerous. Every community sorts the world, and rules gather round whatever will not sit in one division of the sorting. The rule guards the scheme.

paragraph_journey.role: The decisive evidence, and how rules end
paragraph_journey.note: Mourners, brides and returning travellers attract the same rules where no illness is even alleged. And the rules fade when the classification stops organising anything, not when the thing is shown to be safe.
The account can be fitted to anything afterwards. It is worth having only when the scheme is worked out first, from language or household or calendar, and the prohibitions are then predicted.

mentor.tone_progression: Generous while the rival is described, briskly dismissive through the three objections, confident and expansive while the thesis and its evidence are laid out, and then unexpectedly severe at the close, where the author holds his own account to a standard most of its users have not met.
key_transitions: 'It does not survive even a glance at the lists.' (opening of paragraph 2): the received account is refused, and the refusal is argued in three parts.
'The pattern becomes visible as soon as one asks not what is dangerous but what is anomalous.' (opening of paragraph 3): the question is changed and the thesis arrives.
'The account has a weakness of its own, and it is not the one usually brought against it.' (opening of paragraph 5): the author turns on his own explanation.
mentor.misunderstanding: Two pictures form wrongly. The first keeps the hygiene account alive alongside the new one, so that a reader treats the passage as saying taboos are partly about health and partly about categories; the second paragraph does not allow that, since its objections are about the pattern rather than about particular items. The second wrong picture takes the final paragraph as a withdrawal. It is not. It is a condition on the evidence, and the passage says that where the condition has been met the account has often predicted correctly.
mentor.traps_summary: The options here offer the rejected explanation as the author's, invent comparisons between communities or histories the passage never gives, mistake what ends a prohibition, and support the case against the rival where the case for the thesis was asked for. Each is answered by deciding which of the two accounts an option belongs to, and then which claim of the thesis it touches.
mentor.reading_lesson: When an author replaces one explanation with another, keep a two-column note as you read: what is offered against the old account, and what is offered for the new one. Evidence against a rival is not evidence for a survivor, and questions in passages of this shape are built almost entirely on that confusion. The habit also keeps a final self-criticism in its place, as a condition on the new account rather than as a retreat from it.
mentor.real_world: The same test applies to any explanation that can be fitted to a case after the fact, from readings of a market's movements to accounts of why an organisation failed: ask whether the framework could have been stated first and the outcome predicted from it.
mentor.takeaway: An explanation that could have been fitted to any answer has not explained this one.
mentor.reflection_question: Which of the rules you keep without questioning would look strange to someone who did not share the categories they protect?

eli10.big_idea: Rules against certain foods or touching guard how a community sorts the world, not health; but the idea counts only if it predicts.
eli10.story: Why do some groups forbid certain foods? Many people think it is old health advice. Long ago someone got sick, and the warning became a rule. The writer says the lists do not fit. Many forbidden things are safe, and many dangerous things are allowed. So ask a different question: what does not fit? Every group sorts the world into boxes, like a cupboard with labelled shelves. Rules gather around things that sit between shelves. A water animal that breathes air is one. The same rules appear for people between boxes, like a bride moving between two homes. Nobody thinks a bride is catching. And these rules fade when the boxes stop mattering, not when the thing is proved safe. Then the writer warns: you can fit this idea to anything afterwards. It only counts if you work out the boxes first and then predict the rules.
paragraphs: States the usual view: food and contact rules are forgotten health advice from careful ancestors.
Rejects it: lists ignore danger, the least exposed keep rules strictest, and real safety is taught as skill.
Gives the thesis: rules gather round whatever will not fit one box in the community's sorting.
Adds support: people between categories get the same rules, and rules fade when the sorting stops mattering.
Admits a weakness: the idea fits anything afterwards, so it counts only when it predicts in advance.
eli10.author_view: The writer is confident in his account yet strict with it, setting it a hard test rather than abandoning it.
